extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent prosecutors / patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and drafting claims for compliance with 35 U.S.C. §112, second paragraph (definiteness), including tests, common problematic claim language, and examiner procedures when making indefiniteness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory text: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: “The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the textual statutory requirement that underlies definiteness analysis; all claim drafting and examination for indefiniteness is measured against this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The primary purpose of the definiteness requirement for claim language is to ensure that the scope of the claims is clear so that the public is informed of the boundaries of what constitutes infringement of the patent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing definiteness, consider whether the public can determine the claim boundaries; clarity as to scope is the core policy goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be precise, clear, correct and unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: “An essential purpose of patent examination is to fashion claims that are precise, clear, correct, and unambiguous. Only in this way can uncertainties of claim scope be removed, as much as possible, during the administrative process.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should work to remove uncertainties in claim scope during examination; applicants should draft to achieve these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two separate requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: “…the claims must set forth the subject matter that applicants regard as their invention; and the claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter that will be protected by the patent grant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) claiming what the inventor regards as the invention and (b) defining clear metes and bounds of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for definiteness (POSITA in light of specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The test for definiteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112, second paragraph, is whether 'those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read claims in view of the disclosure; apply the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) as of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze definiteness in context (three-part lens)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Definiteness of claim language must be analyzed, not in a vacuum, but in light of: (A) the content of the particular application disclosure; (B) the teachings of the prior art; and (C) the claim interpretation that would be given by one possessing the ordinary level of skill in the pertinent art at the time the invention was made.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider specification disclosure, prior art teachings, and POSITA understanding together when evaluating indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: “USPTO personnel are to give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the supporting disclosure. During patent examination the pending claims must be interpreted as broadly as their terms reasonably allow.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) standard when deciding if multiple plausible constructions exist; BRI can expand claim scope for indefiniteness and art rejection analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim amenable to two or more plausible constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: “If claim is amenable to two or more plausible constructions, applicant is required to amend claim to more precisely define metes and bounds of claimed invention or claim is indefinite under § 112, ¶ 2.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple plausible meanings exist, examiners should require amendment (or issue a 112(2) rejection) rather than assume a narrower meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a claim is subject to more than one interpretation and at least one renders unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Where the claim is subject to more than one interpretation and at least one interpretation would render the claim unpatentable over the prior art, examiner should reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and should reject the claim over the prior art based on the interpretation of the claim that renders the prior art applicable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should (A) issue a 112(2) rejection and (B) enter a prior-art rejection based on the interpretation that would make the claim unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importing limitations from the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: “Limitations appearing in the specification but not recited in the claim should not be read into the claim. . . . Claims must be interpreted 'in view of the specification' without importing limitations from the specification into the claims unnecessarily.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not inject unrecited spec limitations into claim scope; use specification to inform meaning but not to rewrite claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must state reasons when making 112(2) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: “If upon review of a claim in its entirety, the examiner concludes that a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is appropriate, such a rejection should be made and an analysis as to why the phrase(s) used in the claim is ‘vague and indefinite’ should be included in the Office action.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office actions must explain why language is vague/indefinite, citing specific claim phrases and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain whether rejection is indefiniteness or failure to claim what applicant regards as invention
rubrics_metrics.description: “If a rejection is based on 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner should further explain whether the rejection is based on indefiniteness or on the failure to claim what applicants regard as their invention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate and explicitly state the basis—indefiniteness (scope unclear) vs. failure to claim applicant's invention (doesn't claim subject matter applicant regards as invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's traverse/arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: “If applicants traverse the rejection, with or without the submission of an amendment, and the examiner considers applicant’s arguments to be persuasive, the examiner should indicate in the next Office communication that the previous rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, has been withdrawn and provide an explanation as to what prompted the change in the examiner’s position.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner is persuaded, withdraw the 112(2) rejection and explain the change in the next communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se rules — fact specific inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: “Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections. Examples of claim language which have been held to be indefinite set forth in MPEP § 2173.05(d) are fact specific and should not be applied as per se rules.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid categorical black-letter rules; analyze each claim on its facts and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth is not the same as indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Breadth of a claim is not to be equated with indefiniteness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad claim can still be definite; undue breadth may be addressed under other statutes (e.g., 102/103, enablement), not automatically under 112(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between 112(2) rejections and art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: “When making a rejection over prior art in these circumstances, it is important for the examiner to point out how the claim is being interpreted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issuing art rejections where interpretation matters, clearly state the claim construction used and, if ambiguity exists, consider separate 112(2) and art rejections as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base art rejection on speculation about meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: “[A] rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should not be based on considerable speculation about the meaning of terms employed in a claim or assumptions that must be made as to the scope of the claims.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim interpretation is highly uncertain, avoid relying on speculative constructions for obviousness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting claim language vs rejecting
rubrics_metrics.description: “Examiners are encouraged to suggest claim language to applicants to improve the clarity or precision of the language used, but should not reject claims or insist on their own preferences if other modes of expression selected by applicants satisfy the statutory requirement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant's wording meets 112(2), examiner should suggest improvements without issuing a rejection based on stylistic preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments must not introduce new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: “35 U.S.C. 132(a) provides that '[n]o amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When requiring or suggesting claim amendments to cure indefiniteness, ensure amendments do not add new subject matter beyond the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form objection vs substantive rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the form of the claim (as distinguished from its substance) is improper, an 'objection' is made. The practical difference between a rejection and an objection is that a rejection, involving the merits of the claim, is subject to review by the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences, while an objection, if persisted, may be reviewed only by way of petition to the Director of the USPTO.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objections for formal claim problems (form), and rejections for substantive issues (merits); procedural remedies differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims are proper
rubrics_metrics.description: “A product-by-process claim, which is a product claim that defines the claimed product in terms of the process by which it is made, is proper.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product-by-process format is acceptable; evaluate definiteness in light of statutory and case law guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to limitations in another claim is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: “A claim which makes reference to a preceding claim to define a limitation is an acceptable claim construction which should not necessarily be rejected as improper or confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencing earlier claims (e.g., 'product produced by the method of claim 1') is permissible, provided the referenced claim is clear and not ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to cancelled claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Claim 1 cancelled; Claim 2 refers to product produced by method of claim 1 — “Claim 2 should [be] rejected under 35 USC 112 2nd using FP 7.34.01 and then examined under remaining statutes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim depending on a canceled claim is defective and should be rejected under 112(2) (lack of antecedent/definition) and examined for other statutory problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to withdrawn claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Claim depending on a withdrawn claim — “Claim 2 should be objected to for depending upon a withdrawn claim ... Appropriate correction is required.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim depends on a withdrawn claim, treat as an informality (objection) requiring correction rather than a substantive 112 rejection initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim must further limit the independent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Claim 1 recites full SEQ ID; Claim 2 recites fragment — Claim 2 should be objected to for not further limiting claim 1 pursuant to 37 CFR 1.75(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dependent claim that is broader than its independent claim (i.e., does not further limit) is improper in form and should be objected to or amended to proper dependent or independent form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: introducing 'translator controller' then later referring to 'the linear translator' creates ambiguity whether they are same or different elements — 'The claim is ambiguous and a rejection under 35 U.S.C 112, second paragraph based upon a lack of proper antecedent basis is appropriate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each claimed element has proper antecedent basis; unclear references can warrant a 112(2) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single claim mixing product and process (product + use) is indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: “A single claim which claims both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not combine apparatus and usage steps in a single claim; separate apparatus and method claims are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Use’ claims lacking essential steps are indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: “Attempts to claim a process without setting forth any steps involved in the process generally raises an issue of indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely recite a 'use' without active steps (e.g., 'use of X to isolate Y') may be indefinite; consider alternative rejections under 101 or 112 for missing essential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble effect: preamble can be sufficient in process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'A method of treating diabetes comprising administering compound X to a subject in need thereof.' — This claim is considered complete with respect to 35 USC 112 2nd paragraph; no requirement that a preamble need be repeated in a final 'wherein' clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preamble that states intended use/field does not necessarily render the claim indefinite; analyze completeness in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exemplary language ('for example', 'such as') can create indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'A composition comprising Product X and a protease, for example, chymotrypsin.' — Because protease (generic) and chymotrypsin (specific) are not identical in scope, the phrase 'for example' raises the question as to which term is required by the claim; 'the phrase "for example" renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous 'exemplary' phrasing in claims; if used, clarify whether the example is limiting or illustrative, otherwise 112(2) rejection may be warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims using 'derivative thereof' require clear definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples 5A–5C: Claims reciting 'SEQ ID NO:1 or a derivative thereof' may be indefinite if 'derivatives' are not clearly defined in the specification or prior art; but if derivatives are well known or defined, a 112(2) rejection may not be warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming 'derivative' or similar open-ended terms, ensure the specification or common knowledge supplies adequate boundaries; otherwise issue 112(2) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Derived from’ may be acceptable if supported by specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'neural stem cells derived from a spinal cord.' If the specification teaches isolation/derivation from spinal cord, no 112(2) issue arises despite broad claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context and specification support can make broad 'derived from' language definite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical claims: lack of full structure does not automatically render indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: “A claim to a chemical compound is not indefinite merely because a structure is not presented or because a partial structure is presented. Chemical compounds may be claimed by a name that adequately describes the material to one skilled in the art. A compound of unknown structure may be claimed by a combination of physical and chemical characteristics. . . . A compound may also be claimed in terms of the process by which it is made without raising an issue of indefiniteness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate chemical claims in light of whether POSITA can ascertain the claimed compound from names, characteristics, or process descriptions; missing structure alone is not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undefined variables in chemical formulae are indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 7A: Claim with formula where variable 'Z' is not defined in the claim or specification — 'Reject Claim 1 under 35 U.S.C 112 2nd paragraph.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If variables in a claimed formula are not defined or bounded in the specification, issue 112(2) rejection; if spec defines variable (Example 7B), no rejection is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language acceptable when boundaries set
rubrics_metrics.description: “A functional limitation is an attempt to define something by what it does, rather than by what it is ... There is nothing inherently wrong with defining some part of an invention in functional terms. Functional language does not, in and of itself, render a claim improper.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess functional limitations by context, specification support, and POSITA knowledge. Functional language that sets definite boundaries (e.g., known chemical functional definitions) may be allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples where functional chemical limitation was acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Limitation defining a radical as 'incapable of forming a dye with said oxidizing developing agent' was acceptable because it set definite boundaries on the patent protection sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional statements that provide clear, art-understandable boundaries can be definite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical ranges: nested narrow range within broad range in same claim is indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: “Use of a narrow numerical range that falls within a broader range in the same claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries of the claim are not discernible. ... A broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation that falls within the broad range or limitation (in the same claim) is considered indefinite, since the resulting claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the patent protection desired.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming overlapping/nested ranges in the same claim; disclose ranges properly in spec and claim boundaries clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses: permitted when synonymous, problematic when mixing scopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 13: 'glycerol (glycerin)' permitted because terms are identical in scope. Example 14: 'protease (chymotrypsin)' problematic because generic and specific terms differ in scope — 'the use of parentheses raises the question as to which term is required by the claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parentheses only when the parenthetical term is an exact synonym; mixed-scope parentheses can create indefiniteness and merit 112(2) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of trademarks in claims is improper
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 15: Claim reciting 'Velcro attachment' — trademarks identify source, not goods; 'a trademark or trade name is used to identify a source of goods, and not the goods themselves. Thus, a trademark or trade name does not identify or describe the goods associated with the trademark or trade name.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use trademarks/trade names as claim limitations to identify materials/products; such usage is improper and should be objected to/rejected.
